newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK politician urges civil service to stay neutral.
newsitem.headline: HK politician urges civil service to stay neutral.

text.p: A leading Hong Kong politician urged the territory's 180,000-strong civil service on Sunday to be politically neutral as the British colony approaches its return to Chinese rule at midnight June 30.

Legislator Allen Lee, chairman of the pro-China Liberal Party, also claimed the civil service has been politicised in the row over an interim lawmaking chamber that China would install from July 1 in place of the current elected council.

"I have always maintained that the civil service should be politically neutral. Unfortunately, as we witness events...in (the) last few years, no one can deny that the civil service has been politicised," Lee said over government-funded radio.
"To this date, they still have to say in public that the provisional legislature is not necessary. Yet, after 1977, they have to work with the provisional legislature," he said.
The 60-member provisional legislature, formed in December under close supervision by Beijing, would replace Hong Kong's current elected legislative council at the handover.

The move was engineered by Beijing to reverse electoral reforms introduced unilaterally by British Governor Chris Patten in recent years. It is opposed by the Hong Kong government, which has said repeatedly it would not cooperate with the new body.
The new chamber has also led to deep schisms in the current Legco, with 33 incumbent legislators having been selected as members of the post-handover chamber.

Incumbent Legco president Andrew Wong, who made a U-turn from opposing the provisional legislature in 1995 to now vying to become its president, has been denounced by some members of the present council. Some have called for his resignation.
But Wong said on Sunday he had not yet received any formal request from his council colleagues for him to quit.

"I wouldn't respond to any comments by members of the council through the media addressed to me. They must be either taken up with me privately or in written communication," Wong said on government-funded radio.
